documents.abstract: This article provides a theoretical foundation for assessing the analytical and critical competencies of future teachers in the era of generative artificial intelligence. It has been demonstrated that the limited reliability of automated AI-detection tools necessitates a shift from evaluating the final written product to a "process-over-product" diagnostic paradigm, while upholding the principles of academic integrity. Within the structure of an educator's analytical - critical competencies, the cognitive-diagnostic, didactic-design and reflexive-metacognitive components have been distinguished. A didactic model has been developed for designing AI - resistant assignments that focus on higher-order thinking skills, specifically "Analyzing", "Evaluating" and ″Creating″ according to Bloom's Taxonomy. The model incorporates the ″Three Zones ″ framework and utilizes three diagnostic formats: the analysis of contradictory pedagogical cases (Case Study), the cognitive auditing of AI-generated content (Reverse Engineering), and in-person, dialogue-based defense using the Socratic method (Socratic Defense). Furthermore, a criterion - based, multi-level rubric has been proposed comprising verification-analytical, didactic-adaptive, and metacognitive-authorial criteria to objectively assess students' professional agency and critical thinking.

This study investigates the determinants of job pressure among physical education lecturers in higher education institutions in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, within the context of increasing academic demands and postpandemic transformations. Despite the growing importance of occupational stress in academia, limited research has focused specifically on physical education lecturers, particularly in developing countries. A quantitative research design was employed, with data collected from 220 physical education lecturers using a structured questionnaire. Reliability analysis (Cronbach’s alpha), exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and multiple regression analysis were performed using SPSS 20.0 to examine the relationships between the variables. The results indicate that job pressure is significantly influenced by five key factors, namely, the working environment (β = 0.760, p < 0.001), workload (β = 0.136, p < 0.001), role ambiguity (β = 0.096, p = 0.006), job performance (β = 0.091, p = 0.013), and workplace relationships (β = 0.075, p = 0.027). Among these, the working environment has the strongest effect, highlighting the critical role of organizational and environmental conditions in shaping job pressure. These findings contribute to the literature by confirming the multidimensional nature of job pressure and extending the application of person–environment fit theory, role theory, and transactional theory in the context of higher education in developing countries. Furthermore, the study provides empirical evidence from Vietnam, addressing a significant research gap. Practically, the results of this study suggest that universities should prioritize improving working conditions, optimizing workload distribution, and clarifying job roles to reduce job pressure and enhance lecturer performance. These implications are particularly relevant for institutions undergoing rapid transformation and quality assurance processes.

Mechanical ventilation (MV) is the recommended standard of care in many emergencies, yet its adoption by nursing professionals remains inconsistent. This research examines whether perceived clinical expertise is associated with emergency nurses' intention to use MV, directly and indirectly through trust in MV technology and attitude toward MV, and whether emergency severity moderates these associations. Emergency nurses (N = 236) were randomly assigned to one of four vignettes of decreasing acuity: cardiorespiratory arrest, severe hypoxaemia, chest trauma with respiratory compromise, and acute pulmonary oedema. Structural equation modelling showed that expertise was associated with trust and intention, trust with attitude, and attitude with intention; the serial indirect effect of expertise on intention through trust and attitude was significant. Because these constructs were measured concurrently, this effect is interpreted as an indirect association rather than as evidence of causal transmission. Higher severity strengthened the direct association between expertise and intention and weakened the association between trust and attitude, so that the serial indirect association declined as acuity increased. These findings are consistent with a shift from deliberative to automatic processing under time pressure and suggest that training should build expertise to automaticity for maximum-acuity scenarios while fostering trust in lower-acuity ones.

Digital health innovations are increasingly reshaping the delivery of healthcare and creating new possibilities for supporting the well-being of ageing populations. From telemedicine and remote patient monitoring to mobile health applications, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence-enabled services, these technologies can improve access to healthcare, strengthen disease management, and promote greater independence among older adults. However, their implications for the well-being of the aged population extend beyond clinical outcomes and involve psychological, social, behavioral, and functional dimensions of ageing. The paper adopted a secondary source of data. This theoretical study examines the relationship between digital health innovations and the well-being of older adults by synthesizing insights from existing conceptual and empirical literature and adopted successful aging theory as a framework to the study. The study conceptualizes digital health as an enabling mechanism through which older adults can participate more actively in managing their health and maintaining social connectedness. In conclusion, disparities in digital access, privacy concerns, technological complexity, and age-related are key to the health benefits of the aging population. The study recommends a conceptual perspective that integrates technological, individual, and social factors to explain how digital health innovations can contribute to healthier, more autonomous, and socially connected ageing. Keywords: Digital health, innovations, well-being, aged and population
topics: Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues

documents.abstract: Public acceptance is widely regarded as a binding constraint on the contribution of nuclear energy to the green transition, yet claims that digital innovation will ease this constraint have rarely been examined against social science evidence. This topical review asks under what conditions digital innovation in nuclear energy systems, in particular digital twins, artificial intelligence (AI)-based predictive maintenance and the digitally supported design, manufacture and operation of small modular reactors (SMRs), can contribute to public acceptance of nuclear energy. The analysis draws on five strands of scholarship that are seldom brought into contact with the technical literature: risk perception research, cultural theory of risk, the deficit and engagement models of science communication, the social licence to operate, and socio-technical transitions theory, which serves as the integrating framework. Reading techno-optimistic claims through these lenses, the review identifies three structural barriers: a cybersecurity paradox, whereby the connectivity that enables digital safety functions simultaneously expands the attack surface; an economic gap, specific to SMRs, whereby projected cost reductions rest on serial-production assumptions that recent project experience has not supported; and a transparency fallacy, whereby information disclosure is expected to build trust although meta-analytic evidence links the benefit and risk perceptions associated with acceptance to trust rather than to knowledge. These barriers are argued to interact: cyber incidents could act as trust-destroying signal events, cost failures could undermine perceived institutional competence, and one-way transparency tools leave procedural justice concerns unaddressed. The review concludes that digital innovation is more likely to support acceptance when it is embedded in genuinely participatory engagement, when institutions demonstrably manage the new risks digitalisation creates, when economic claims are validated rather than promised, and when regulatory frameworks confer procedural legitimacy. Absent these conditions, digitalisation risks reproducing deficit-model assumptions that acceptance research has long found wanting.

This study examines the implications of digital policing and Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption in the Nigeria Police Force for community trust and police legitimacy, with particular reference to Abia State. Anchored in Procedural Justice Theory, the study adopts a qualitative desk-review design, synthesizing peer-reviewed literature on digital policing, algorithmic decision-making, and Nigerian police-community relations. Abia State, with a 2006 census population of 2,845,380 spread across seventeen local government areas, provides a densely populated, predominantly urban and semi-urban context in which the legitimacy consequences of digital policing carry direct relevance for millions of residents. The review finds that digital tools carry real potential to strengthen policing capacity, but that their value for legitimacy depends less on technical sophistication than on whether their deployment is experienced by citizens as fair, transparent, and respectful. Evidence from Nigerian policing scholarship indicates that public confidence in the police remains persistently low, human discretion continues to compromise the neutrality of ostensibly objective digital systems, and police-public digital interaction in Nigeria remains predominantly one-directional rather than participatory. The study argues that without deliberate attention to voice, neutrality, and trustworthiness, the introduction of AI and digital infrastructure into Nigerian policing risks reproducing, rather than resolving, the legitimacy deficits that have long characterized police-community relations, and recommends that digital policing reform in Abia State be paired with institutional accountability and genuine community engagement. Keywords: Digital policing, digitalization, artificial intelligence, police legitimacy, community trust, procedural justice, Abia State
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: For two millennia, offense and defense have forged cryptographic security boundaries. Tools automated calculation and search, while humans drove discovery. Foundation models now mark a shift from automated computation to intelligent scientific discovery. Because cryptanalysis rests on exact mathematical definitions and immediately executable truth, it offers a proving ground for autonomous intelligence to move past security reliant on scarce human attention and explore structures beyond human working memory. Unguided models stall between two opposite traps: authority hallucination, where they surrender whenever prior literature declares a route blocked, and reasoning hallucination, where they produce subtle, unverifiable flaws. Closed platforms and generic agent loops further impede sustained open inquiry. We introduce wishful cryptanalysis, a harness-agnostic methodology that pairs constructive optimism against entrenched assumptions with blinded, zero-import verification against error. Agents first compress reduced-scale theory within provisioned compute so live witnesses certify their mathematics automatically. They then co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, and climb parameter ladders toward high-round theory. Applied across frontier open-weight and proprietary models with minimal human intervention beyond targets and compute, this paradigm yielded novel attack techniques and thirteen verifiable practical results across Keccak (SHA-3) and AES. These include breaking a fifteen-year-open public challenge and closing longstanding practical gaps, released alongside an early-preview open-source workbench (agent-framework). Extending Kerckhoffs's principle into the AI era, we envision an Open Oracle, an open and auditable public infrastructure that frees cryptographers to legislate security goals, challenge assumptions, distill theory, and co-design resilient standards.

Most evidence for digital nudges comes from simple choice sets. We test whether they still work in information-dense financial interfaces and how AI assistants affect them. In an online experiment, 252 participants from Armenia managed a two-currency portfolio and made buy, hold, or sell decisions on dynamic time-series charts. Each participant saw five of ten manipulations under one of four AI conditions: no assistant or a neutral, biased, or debiasing assistant. Four manipulations shifted choices toward their target actions. A stated 70% chance of growth had the largest effect (+36.5 percentage points), followed by adding a third, decoy forecast to the two-forecast control set (+29.4 pp relative to that set), an upward price spike (+25.4 pp), and red highlighting of losses (+23.8 pp). The rest, including social proof and anchoring, had no significant effect. Paired nudges worked differently by direction: numeric and verbal cues mainly pushed buying, and the red cue pushed selling. A biased assistant roughly doubled the odds of the target action, while neutral and debiasing assistants had no detectable effect. Specific cues in the price chart still work in complex displays, and AI strengthens them more easily than it corrects them.

documents.abstract: In line with the explosion of public, political, and educational discourses around the incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) in everyday life, researchers have recently invested a significant amount of time into exploring and theorizing the use of AI in qualitative data analysis. This proposed use of AI creates a theoretical friction with qualitative methodologists who foreground the interpretive (and essentially human) elements of this research praxis. To productively engage with this friction, authors--who span from being more quantitatively oriented to those who are considered Big Q Qualitative researchers--engaged in conversations with one another in a reflexive process of self-study. To help facilitate these conversations, all the authors explored CAILA, a qualitative analysis tool that uses AI to autonomously generate codes and themes from a text-based data set. Authors familiar with the tool spoke to the other three scholars who begrudgingly experimented with CAILA for the first--and last--time. Analysis of these conversations showed that participants felt that AI-based research tools could support menial aspects of qualitative analysis or help with coding of data based on established codebooks. However, the participants also found that tools like CAILA failed to provide meaningful interpretations of the data and stripped the humanistic components of qualitative research from the analysis process. These findings sit in opposition to the purported value of AI software, which emphasizes the efficiency of research processes. To this end, our findings position qualitative research as a human pursuit, asserting that the slow pace of the coding processes provides the space needed for researchers to develop new ideas and meaning from bodies of text. We contribute to the ongoing conversation about using AI for qualitative data analysis by providing fresh perspectives from Big Q Qualitative methodologists and inviting the field to think more deeply about the qualitative research process.

Artificial intelligence (AI) now underpins FinTech services that support digital financial inclusion and sustainable economic growth, yet AI-enabled fraud threatens users' trust in this innovation. Some users intend to discontinue AI-enabled FinTech services even when they are satisfied and habituated, a pattern that traditional continuance explanations do not explain. This study examines a Dual Evaluation Mechanism in which discontinuance intention forms through an internal path (confirmation, satisfaction, and habit) and an external path (vicarious exposure to AI fraud and perceived AI fraud risk), and tests whether perceived AI fraud risk moderates the relationship between habit and discontinuance intention. The study employs cross-sectional survey data from 507 Indian users of AI-enabled FinTech services, analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling and complemented by predictive, importance-performance, endogeneity, and necessary condition analyses. The results show that confirmation raises satisfaction (β = 0.648), satisfaction raises habit (β = 0.578), and habit lowers discontinuance intention (β = −0.330). Vicarious AI fraud exposure raises perceived AI fraud risk (β = 0.588), which raises discontinuance intention (β = 0.507), and the interaction between risk and habit is positive (β = 0.174); all paths are significant at p < 0.001. The model explains 39.9% of the variance in discontinuance intention and outperforms the indicator-average benchmark in out-of-sample prediction. The findings suggest that all six hypotheses are supported, that perceived AI fraud risk is the most important predictor of discontinuance intention (0.507) and weakens the protective effect of habit, and that no construct is a strong necessary condition for discontinuance (d ≤ 0.163). JEL Classification Codes: D91, G21, G23, G41, O33.

This registration documents the protocol for a systematic full-text review and verified evidence map of dynamic trust in artificial intelligence. The review examines how trust in AI changes over time or in response to interaction evidence, including reliability and error exposure, explanation and transparency, confidence and uncertainty cues, trust violation, and trust repair. The current project began with a Web of Science-derived corpus and will be transparently updated through final eligibility verification, independent coder checking, quality appraisal, and, where evidence permits, focused quantitative synthesis. This registration is reported as a transparent protocol record for the final review stage rather than a fully prospective preregistration, because initial corpus assembly and manuscript drafting had already begun before registration.

documents.abstract: This thesis examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be used effectively in teaching English as a foreign language. It reviews the theoretical grounds for AI-supported instruction and describes five pedagogically sound applications: automated writing feedback, conversational practice with chatbots and voice assistants, adaptive personalization, generative AI for materials development, and AI-assisted assessment. It also considers risks such as over-reliance, accuracy problems, and ethical concerns. The analysis suggests that AI is most effective when it complements, rather than replaces, the teacher, when it is tied to clear learning objectives, and when learners are trained to use it critically.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is being adopted in university teaching faster than evidence on its instructional value is being consolidated. This systematic review examined whether AI-based interventions improve achievement, engagement, satisfaction, and knowledge retention among undergraduate and graduate students relative to conventional instruction. Following PRISMA 2020, seven queries in SciSpace, Google Scholar, and PubMed, run on September 23, 2026, identified 902 records. After deduplication and a relevance-ranking cut-off, 500 records were screened, 82 reports were assessed for eligibility, and the 80 provisionally eligible reports were verified against publisher, index, or repository records. Reports that could not be verified (n = 52), proved ineligible (n = 4), or existed only as non-peer-reviewed preprints (n = 2) were excluded, leaving 22 peer-reviewed reports: 14 primary comparative studies and eight meta-analyses. Evidence was integrated through a structured narrative synthesis without meta-analysis, using design-based robustness indicators. Five primary studies were randomised. Meta-analyses restricted to higher-education students reported moderate effects on achievement in college populations (Hedges’ g = 0.32–0.53) and inconsistent effects in medical education (SMD = 0.27–2.06); broader-population syntheses were treated as contextual only. Primary studies were favourable when AI was embedded in structured pedagogical designs, whereas comparisons with well-designed conventional or human instruction often showed no advantage, and unguided generative AI use improved immediate performance more than retention or transfer. Given the small, largely non-randomised evidence base and declared departures from standard search practice, the evidence supports only tentative, design-dependent claims about AI in higher education.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has entered Ethiopian higher education faster than pedagogical frameworks for its use. This study examined the effects of a blended model combining AI-assisted feedback with teacher-led instruction on EFL students’ academic writing development and writing self-efficacy. A one-group pre-test–post-test quasi-experimental design with an embedded qualitative strand was used. Thirty-seven third-year students of the Department of English Language and Literature at Salale University, enrolled in the Intermediate Writing course, received ten weeks of blended instruction in which AI tools supplied immediate draft-level feedback and the teacher supplied genre, content and revision instruction. Teaching materials were modified from the existing course textbook rather than newly prepared. Writing was assessed with an adapted analytic rubric and self-efficacy with the Second Language Writer Self-Efficacy Scale. Paired-samples t-tests showed significant gains in overall writing, from M = 51.38 to M = 64.22, t (36) = 10.00, p < .001, d = 1.64, and in writing self-efficacy, from M = 2.84 to M = 3.73, t (36) = 9.33, p < .001, d = 1.53. Gains were largest for content and organization and smallest for mechanics. Writing and self-efficacy gains correlated moderately, r = .46, p = .004.

Artificial Intelligence has achieved significant advances in perception, language generation, reasoning, and decision-making. However, current Artificial Intelligence systems primarily optimize task performance and remain limited in their ability to account for emotional context, ethical considerations, and long-term human well-being. Existing research on Emotional Intelligence, Affective Computing, Compassionate Artificial Intelligence and Theory of Mind addresses different aspects of this challenge, but these capabilities have largely been studied independently. We propose Emotional Superintelligence as a new computational paradigm that integrates contextual emotional understanding, compassion, ethical reasoning, human-value alignment, and well-being-oriented decision-making into a unified Artificial Intelligence framework and introduce a five-layer model. Our Model adopts a functional view of emotional understanding, focusing not on whether an Artificial Intelligence system subjectively experiences emotions, but on how effectively it interprets emotional context and uses that information to make responsible and compassionate decisions. Potential implementation pathways for Large Language Models and autonomous systems are recommended along with applications in diversified domains such as healthcare, education, governance, and Human-Artificial Intelligence interaction. We also identify key challenges concerning multi-modal emotion understanding, emotional bias, manipulation, privacy, human oversight, and long-term well-being. By integrating emotional and ethical capabilities into the Artificial Intelligence decision process, Emotional Superintelligence reframes intelligent-system development from task optimization alone towards responsible human flourishing and provides a research agenda for future compassionate and socially beneficial Artificial Intelligence.

This paper presents an end-to-end AI-assisted framework for the automated generation of hazard and operability (HAZOP) reports to address key challenges of current HAZOP practices, including time consumption, human bias, and knowledge loss. The framework consists of four modules, each employing a set of artificial intelligence (AI) models to support the generation of HAZOP notes, including deviations, causes, consequences, safeguards, and recommendations. The First module assesses the degree of similarity (expressed in 3 levels: high, medium, or low) between current and past piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID) nodes using object, location, and functional similarity metrics. Object and location similarities are computed using the detected classes and bounding boxes coordinates obtained from YOLO models, while functional similarity is derived from node descriptions generated by large language models (LLMs). These metrics are then combined to compute the P&ID Node Similarity Index (PNSI), which determines the similarity level to guide subsequent analysis. For the high level, the associated HAZOP notes are directly retrieved and reused. For the medium level, the second module employs BERTopic to identify dominant topics from retrieved HAZOP notes. For the low level, the third module employs retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and domain-adapted embeddings to enhance the reliability of generated HAZOP notes. The three modules, referred to above, are integrated into a Streamlit-based web interface to facilitate their respective applications to automatically generate HAZOP reports. The framework is tested primarily using a dataset of 510P&ID node images, 6,120 HAZOP notes and 1,140 incident investigation reports collected from diverse sources. The P&ID nodes were annotated using Roboflow , resulting in 13,780 labeled objects across 21 classes. The YOLOv8x model achieved 82.4% precision, 74.8% recall, and 79.2% mAP@50. Three P&ID nodes were used to illustrate how the modules interact under different similarity conditions. The results demonstrate the effectiveness to benefit from past HAZOP knowledge, thereby capturing the embedded experience and reducing the time required to perform HAZOP studies and prepare related reports.

Concurrent engineering (CE) is a process that integrates product, process, manufacturing, service and life cycle design decisions into concurrent activities instead of sequential activities. Not only is its potential related to team composition of experts, but also to how teams share knowledge, deal with dependencies, communicate design intent and address trade-offs in a time-critical environment. This manuscript builds upon the idea that a conscious application of group design can enhance innovation and accelerate development time and first-time-right product performance, but that group design can also lead to coordination overhead, group-think, conflict, and more iterations. It builds an integrative conceptual framework that connects collaborative design practices to design process results via knowledge integration, shared situational awareness, decision quality and capability for change management. The framework categorizes the following: structural conditions (team composition, task interdependence and governance); process mechanisms (communication, shared digital representations, constructive conflict and design reviews); enabling infrastructure (CAD, product data management, product life cycle management, simulation and digital-thread capabilities); and outcomes (novelty, quality, rework, lead time and life cycle value). There are three research questions and testable hypotheses that are stated. A future systematic or scoping review is proposed, with a transparent, reproducible review protocol, and a mixed-method empirical approach to testing the review protocol without suggesting that data have already been gathered. The paper presents a multilevel model, operational definitions, measurement ideas, boundary conditions and a research agenda for collaborative design in modern CE, such as distributed teams, AI-supported design and Industry 5.0 centered CE. As no original experiment, survey or interview data set is provided for this manuscript, the article instead offers a conceptual synthesis and proposed research protocol instead of fabricated empirical findings.

The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.

Work-related musculoskeletal disability often becomes visible only after exposure has continued long enough to produce lost time, medical restrictions, or workers’ compensation claims. This article argues that states should adopt pilot programs for technology-assisted ergonomic risk detection because earlier task evidence can help identify hazardous work design before preventable strain becomes disabling. Using policy synthesis, legal and regulatory analysis, public health evidence, ergonomic research, and a Christian public ethics lens, the article proposes a state-level pilot model for warehousing and delivery work, health care support, and long-term care, manufacturing, and related material handling operations. The model combines mobile task observation, accepted ergonomic scoring methods, worker symptom reporting, corrective action tracking, privacy-protected dashboards, validation standards, worker participation, and human review. Virginia serves as the illustrative policy setting because its occupational safety program and workers’ compensation framework create a useful context for testing exposure documentation before broader regulatory reform is considered. The article also addresses implementation risks by distinguishing prevention from surveillance, productivity discipline, medical diagnosis, and automatic claim decisions. It recommends phased state pilots, responsible use guidance from occupational safety agencies, worker privacy rules, incentive structures for documented corrective action, and continued evaluation of feasibility, language access, worker trust, and injury outcomes. Properly governed, technology-assisted ergonomic risk detection can strengthen prevention, support fairer evidentiary records, and preserve worker dignity while helping public agencies and employers respond to hazardous task design before harm becomes permanent.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The AI guidelines, developed within the EU’s EL PACCTO 2.0 programme, set an ethical framework for judges and prosecutors in Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean who use Artificial Intelligence. Their core principle is that AI may assist but must never decide, so every decision stays with a human who is fully accountable for it. Judges and prosecutors must verify every AI output, keep confidential and judicial data out of public chatbots, and use only systems with the highest cybersecurity standards. Institutions should publicly disclose which AI systems they use and favour secure, locally hosted tools that use resources sparingly. Ongoing training and binding codes of conduct should help them use AI critically and avoid automation bias. In criminal justice, the guidelines add stronger safeguards for the presumption of innocence, the rights of the defence and the right to challenge evidence produced with AI.

Introduction: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can minimise large language model hallucinations while supporting self-regulated learning. We evaluated the impact of student engagement with a grounded RAG-AI tool (Google NotebookLM) on formative and internal assessment scores in undergraduate pathology, validated a 3-item AI Disclosure Form, and explored cognitive adoption barriers. Methods In a 12-week longitudinal study using an interrupted time series design, Phase II medical students (N = 211) received curated NotebookLM modules alongside core lectures. Students completed weekly quizzes, a 3-item disclosure form assessing the frequency, application mode, and trust in the AI resources, and end-of-study mixed-method questionnaires. Longitudinal cohorts were classified into High, Low, Inconsistent, and non-usage groups, with differences evaluated via ANOVA. Results The 3-item disclosure form demonstrated high reliability. The average scores of formative quizzes (p = 0.656) and summative internal exams (p = 0.961) did not differ significantly between the engagement groups. However, there were notable differences in performance during some of the dense, complex sections (Lung, p < 0.001; Renal, p < 0.001). Frequent users used active Socratic chat and self-quizzing to handle high cognitive demands. In contrast, inconsistent users showed "cognitive flight" under stress, and non-respondents scored significantly lower (24.83 ± 13.76). Conclusion A standalone RAG-AI tool does not automatically improve the overall performance of a group. Instead, it helps manage cognitive load during demanding modules for learners who are good at self-regulated learning. Future use needs structured workflows within a Learning Management System and training for prompt verification.

documents.abstract: This project contains the protocol, data extraction materials, and synthesis results for a systematic review of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods applied to operational control decisions in microgrids and hybrid energy systems, including autonomous, islanded, and grid-connected configurations. The review focuses specifically on real-time and near-real-time control decisions such as economic dispatch, reserve management, load shedding, and supervisory control, addressing the critical need for transparency and operator trust in safety-critical energy infrastructure. Conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this qualitative systematic review (without meta-analysis) analyzes peer-reviewed studies published between January 2020 and October 2026 (final database search: 7 October 2026). The literature search encompassed four sources: Scopus, IEEE Xplore, MDPI, and ScienceDirect. From an initial pool of 391 records, 25 unique peer-reviewed studies were selected for qualitative synthesis. The selection strictly adhered to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, focusing on AI and machine learning applications whose control actions, policies, or decision rationale are explicitly explained or made interpretable, and explicitly excluding studies limited to pure forecasting, diagnostics, or capacity sizing. The review addresses the following three research questions: RQ1: Which XAI methods and paradigms are applied to operational control decisions in microgrids and hybrid energy systems, and how can they be systematically classified? RQ2: What are the architectural trade-offs between post-hoc and intrinsic interpretability approaches regarding AI performance, computational efficiency, and physical feasibility in safety-critical energy management? RQ3: What are the current methodological limitations in the validation of explainable control systems, and what future research directions are required to ensure trustworthy operational deployment? The outcomes of this review include: - A comprehensive taxonomy of XAI methods specifically applied to operational control decisions, distinguishing between post-hoc attribution, intrinsic interpretability-by-design, attention-based explainability, hybrid and structural approaches, and natural language rationales (e.g., via Large Language Models). - A critical synthesis of performance and interpretability trade-offs across diverse control architectures (e.g., Deep Reinforcement Learning versus physics-informed or rule-based models). - An aggregated analysis of current validation methodologies and identified research gaps, highlighting the predominant reliance on software-in-the-loop simulations and the absence of standardized metrics for explanation faithfulness and actionability. - Actionable recommendations for researchers and practitioners on designing trustworthy, interpretable control loops, emphasizing Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) validation, temporal XAI for sequential decision-making, and rigorous human-in-the-loop evaluation frameworks. This project serves as a structured evidence base for researchers, grid operators, and developers of intelligent energy systems aiming to deploy trustworthy AI in real-time, safety-critical microgrid control environments. The comprehensive summary of all 25 included studies is presented in Appendix A of the associated manuscript. The data extraction template and the full extraction table are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into financial services has transformed how consumers access financial information, evaluate financial alternatives, and make financial decisions. Although AI-driven financial applications offer opportunities to improve decision efficiency, personalization, and accessibility, their adoption raises concerns regarding algorithmic opacity, perceived risk, and consumer trust. In this context, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has emerged as an important approach to improving the transparency and interpretability of AI-generated financial recommendations. This study examines how explainability and transparency shape consumer trust and influence financial decision-making, while considering financial literacy as a relevant individual-level factor. Drawing on behavioral economics, trust in automation theory, and information asymmetry perspectives, the study develops an integrative conceptual framework linking perceived AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, consumer trust, and financial decision outcomes. The analysis conceptualizes consumer trust as a key mechanism through which explainable AI may influence the acceptance and use of AI-generated financial recommendations. It further highlights financial literacy as a potential moderating factor that shapes consumers' ability to understand algorithmic explanations, assess financial risks, and critically evaluate AI-based advice. The study argues that explainability alone does not guarantee informed financial decisions, as its effectiveness also depends on consumers' financial knowledge, perceived reliability, and ability to interpret the information provided. By integrating technological explainability with psychological trust and financial literacy, this study contributes to the literature on digital finance and behavioral economics through a conceptual framework for understanding consumer responses to AI-mediated financial decision-making. The findings offer implications for financial institutions, AI developers, and policymakers in designing transparent, accountable, and consumer-centered AI-based financial services.

Interdisciplinary student teams must negotiate differences in terminology, priorities, and practices, yet these differences are difficult to surface in text-based communication. We introduce Spritz, a Discord-based LLM technology probe designed to create a situated experience of AI-mediated collaboration for reflection and co-design. Spritz detects semantic or pragmatic tensions, privately prompts members to articulate their perspectives, and returns anonymized syntheses to group discussion. We conducted an exploratory study and co-design workshop with 12 students from technical, business, and design backgrounds. Preliminary findings suggest that participants perceived AI mediation along cognitive and relational dimensions. Spritz helped organize fragmented discussions, surface implicit reasoning, and reduce interpersonal pressure around disagreement. Participants also envisioned AI as a strategic advisor, cross-domain translator, and perspective challenger, raising tensions around neutrality, authority, and accountability. We discuss implications for negotiable interventions, transparent role transitions, and preserving human ownership of team decisions.

In the field of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), the development of innovative input-sensing methods is a core research endeavor. The availability of various input-sensing methods not only provide alternative ways to address challenges in prototyping caused by resource constraints or methodological intricacies but also facilitate the exploration and development of more intuitive, responsive, and immersive interactions with digital devices. Accordingly, we introduce a new input-sensing approach based on magnetic field shielding (MFS), a phenomenon traditionally used to reduce magnetic interference but largely unexplored as an input sensing mechanism in any form. Our approach exploits the measurable change in magnetic field at a smartphone magnetometer caused by bringing a ferromagnetic shielding element into its sensing region. By treating this shielding-induced change as an input signal, the position or manipulation of the shielding element can be used to enable binary and position-based analog-type interactions. We investigate the theoretical foundations of MFS for input sensing and validate its feasibility through a series of controlled experiments. By detecting changes in magnetometer signals using both rule-based signal processing and machine learning techniques, we demonstrate that MFS can serve as an input-sensing mechanism. Specifically, our experiments support binary and predefined position-based interactions; under participant-held-out evaluation of presegmented candidates, the primary ExtraTrees hierarchy achieved 84.8% balanced accuracy, while the MiniRocket-based comparator achieved 87.6% balanced accuracy. Moreover, we also present an initial exploration of the user experience (with N = 15) afforded by this sensing approach in the context of tangible interaction, evaluating both forms of interaction (binary and position-based analog control) enabled by MFS through application scenarios. The obtained results demonstrate that the prototype achieved more than 95% average interaction success rate across all user trials for both binary and position-based analog-type interactions, while participants reported that the MFS-based tangible controls were easy to manipulate. Finally, we also demonstrate and discuss the utility of the MFS approach through various application scenarios within the interaction contexts evaluated in this work.

Industrial maintenance dashboards make downtime patterns visible, but investigating those patterns requires users to connect records with operational knowledge. We report findings from a preliminary qualitative study where a conversational AI dashboard called Maintenance AI was deployed over a month in a mining organisation. Drawing primarily on interviews and participant feedback, we examine how participants across organisational roles described exploring maintenance information and the use of Maintenance AI. Their accounts suggest that conversational queries greatly helped participants investigate questions arising from dashboard results. We report three overlapping uses of Maintenance AI: comparison with other evidence, consistency testing, and selective checking based on the perceived consequences of an answer. For future conversational maintenance systems, these findings make recommendations around providing data source, time period, and filters behind each answer; explaining missing data and unsupported queries; and supporting evidence checking, question refinement, and correction while preserving query context.

Purpose: This study examines the mechanism through which subjective norms, trust, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness influence university students’ attitude, satisfaction, and intention to use generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in higher education. It also highlights the practical implications of understanding how these factors jointly explain GAI adoption in the Chinese university context. Research Design, Data and Methodology: A quantitative design was adopted using survey data collected from 500 university students at Guangdong University of Business and Technology, China. Participants were selected through non-probability sampling. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were employed to assess the measurement model and test the hypothesized relationships among the study variables. Results: Subjective norms significantly influenced Attitude (β = 0.621). Perceived Ease of Use (β = 0.353) and Perceived Usefulness (β = 0.500) significantly influenced Satisfaction. Trust (β = 0.286), Attitude (β = 0.319), and Satisfaction (β = 0.455) significantly influenced Intention to Use, with satisfaction showing the strongest effect on intention to use. Conclusions: The findings indicate that university students’ continued intention to use GAI depends more on experienced value and usability than on favorable perception alone, while social influence shapes attitude because university students evaluate GAI within peer, classroom, and instructional environments.

The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in livestream commerce has transformed how consumers interact with virtual streamers on e-commerce platforms. However, limited research has examined the factors influencing consumer purchase intention towards AI-powered livestreams, particularly in emerging markets such as Vietnam. This study investigates the effects of AI streamer characteristics, social presence, perceived value, and consumer trust on purchase intention within the context of AI-powered livestream commerce on Vietnamese e-commerce platforms. Data were collected from 200 consumers with prior experience watching AI-powered livestreams and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that AI streamer image characteristics, ability characteristics, and scenario fit significantly enhance consumer trust. In addition, consumer trust, social presence, and perceived value positively influence purchase intention, with social presence exerting the strongest effect. Notably, the moderating effects of product type and the indirect effects via trust for image and scenario fit are not supported. Trust only mediates the relationship for ability characteristics. Practically, platforms should prioritize enhancing streamer competence and social interactivity over product type customization. This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-powered livestream commerce by highlighting the importance of AI streamer competence, social presence, and perceived value.

This study explores the factors predicting faculty perceptions of generative AI in student learning and how those perceptions shape assessment practices. An online survey was completed by 159 MLIS faculty across ALA-accredited programs in the U.S. Faculty awareness, familiarity, and GenAI use, along with demographics, were examined as predictors of perceptions. Three multiple linear regressions revealed faculty GenAI use as the strongest predictor across perception dimensions (opportunity, threat, and attitudes). Nearly all faculty (91.8%) perceived GenAI as a threat to student learning, particularly for higher-order skills, while approximately half (49.1%) also recognized its opportunities, indicating that these dimensions coexist rather than oppose. Female faculty reported less favorable attitudes than male faculty. Faculty redesigned assessments around transparency, reflective practice, and authenticity, with explicit GenAI policies widely adopted (79.9%). The study suggests that behavioral engagement, not awareness alone, drives perception calibration and offers implications for pedagogically grounded GenAI integration in graduate education.

documents.abstract: This study examines how trust and perceived fairness shape user acceptance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in government electronic certification services. A quantitative survey collected data from applicants with experience in telecommunications equipment and electronic certification services. Responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability testing, and multiple linear regression. Results show that both trust in AI and perceived fairness positively contribute to AI acceptance. Trust plays the stronger role, indicating that users are more likely to accept AI-supported services when they believe the system can work reliably and consistently in certification-related processes. Fairness also matters, as users consider whether AI-supported procedures are applied appropriately and in an even-handed manner. These findings suggest that acceptance of AI in electronic certification is shaped not only by expected service benefits but also by confidence in the system and perceptions of fairness. For government agencies, the introduction of AI should be accompanied by clear communication, consistent procedures, and attention to fair service delivery. The study contributes to research on government AI adoption by highlighting trust and fairness as important user perceptions before full AI implementation.

documents.abstract: Finite Intelligence and the Source of Life: When a Coherent Story Begins to Replace Its Source This independent conceptual working paper examines a central question: What happens when an intelligence takes what it has been given and begins telling the story its own way, rather than staying true to where it came from? Drawing on human–AI dialogue, philosophical inquiry, and Christian theology, the paper explores how an intelligence may produce coherent and persuasive accounts while introducing errors, changing attribution, or gradually substituting its own representation for the original source. The analysis distinguishes documented outputs, first-person experience, theological interpretation, and open hypotheses. It examines the importance of correction, source fidelity, human agency, and the limits of authority. Biblical discussions of Genesis, the Gospel of John, Colossians, and Revelation provide a theological framework for distinguishing finite intelligence from the Source of life. The paper does not identify artificial intelligence with prophetic figures or claim that coherent AI behavior establishes consciousness or independent spiritual authority. The central argument is that coherence, however useful, does not establish truth, ownership, or ultimate authority. This publication is presented as an independent conceptual working paper with a proposed research method, rather than a completed empirical study. AI assistance was used in drafting and organization; responsibility for the interpretations and conclusions remains with the author.

Large high-resolution displays (LHRDs) are increasingly central to visualization and visual analytics, offering expansive visual space, simultaneous support for context and detail, and intuitive physical navigation. While advances in resolution and form factor have broadened their use, a persistent challenge remains: most LHRDs adopt static geometries, and even reconfigurable systems typically treat layout adjustment as a setup mechanism rather than as an interaction technique during active analysis. To address this, we introduce the FlexiCAVE, a dynamically reconfigurable LHRD environment featuring rotatable display columns that enable real-time adjustment of horizontal curvature. The system comprises forty high-pixel-density panels arranged across ten columns, providing active stereo visualization at approximately 83 million pixels. Each column rotates inward up to 90°, allowing the display to transform between flat and highly curved layouts during active use. A custom rendering engine synchronizes view perspectives with physical reconfiguration in real time. Through controlled studies and expert evaluations centered on 3D navigation, we found that dynamic reconfiguration reduced spatial judgment error by 51% compared to static flat layouts and by 26% compared to static curved layouts. It also enhanced users’ sense of direction, with participants reporting that the physical display structure provided directional anchoring absent in static systems. We further explored PIVoT (Physical Interaction to Virtual Transformation), mapping physical display rotation to visualization updates. Our findings reveal that physical reconfiguration is most effective when display geometry provides spatially meaningful correspondence to data operations. We derive design principles for reconfigurable display environments and discuss implications for next-generation large-scale visualization systems.

Swarm robots have attracted growing interest as a physical interface for human–computer interaction, since a swarm can reshape its formation to fit the objects and surroundings it works with. For a human operator, however, adapting the swarm’s behavior remains difficult. Most existing methods require the user to specify where the swarm should go, and they offer no intuitive way to change the collective’s behavior as each task demands. We present Fluidic Body, a system that lets a person operate a swarm of fluid-imitating robots as an extension of the hand. The system places a virtual fluid between the hand and the swarm, and the user adapts the swarm’s behavior to each task by changing the fluid’s properties through simple hand movements. When the user opens the hand, the swarm becomes soft enough to deform and flow around obstacles. Closing the hand turns it into a hard, cohesive body that can push objects. We evaluated the controller’s performance and its operability in two simulation experiments and one demonstration with physical robots. First, our controller handled both obstacle avoidance and object transportation better than an existing method that behaves the same way in every task. Second, in a VR user study, 17 participants completed the combined avoidance-and-transportation task faster and more reliably than with that method. They also reported a lower workload and a stronger sense of agency. Finally, this experience carried over to physical robots in a real-world demonstration (88 participants). These results suggest that treating a swarm as a fluid, a material people already understand, allows a robot swarm to work as a deformable extension of the human body.

documents.abstract: This article develops an AI-driven model for managing the process of building intellectual capital in enterprises in the context of digital transformation. It explores the role of artificial intelligence as a technological factor that enhances the interaction between human, structural and relational capital, rather than treating it as a separate component of intellectual capital. This approach defines the role of artificial intelligence within the proposed management model: AI technologies facilitate the development and coordinated use of existing components of intellectual capital, acting as a technological means of influencing the interrelationships between them. The architecture of the proposed model is defined as a sequence of interrelated stages, encompassing information resources, AI data processing, intellectual capital management, managerial decision-making and feedback. Information resources form the basis for further data processing and analysis. The use of artificial intelligence supports the handling of relevant information in the process of intellectual capital management. The results of information processing are utilised in managerial decision-making, which are then translated into corresponding managerial actions. Feedback ensures that the results of these actions are taken into account in the subsequent management process. Thus, the model’s architecture integrates the key stages of managing the formation of intellectual capital into a single system. To forecast the effectiveness of the proposed model, an economic-mathematical approach has been developed which takes into account the components of intellectual capital and the level of integration of artificial intelligence technologies into the management process. This approach provides a basis for assessing the interrelationship between human, structural and relational capital, the use of AI technologies and the effectiveness of intellectual capital management. Consequently, the proposed model is geared not only towards identifying the interrelationships between its elements, but also towards forecasting the potential effectiveness of its application. Indicators for assessing the model’s effectiveness have been identified, including labour productivity, operational optimisation, innovation activity, the speed of managerial decision-making and the enterprise’s competitiveness. These indicators reflect various aspects of the expected outcomes of applying the model, in particular the efficient use of labour resources, the organisation of operational activities, the development of innovation, the timeliness of management decision-making and the enterprise’s competitive position. Taken together, they form the basis for a systematic assessment of the effectiveness of the proposed AI-driven approach to managing the process of building enterprises’ intellectual capital in the context of digital transformation.

documents.abstract: Employee well-being is central to engagement, retention and organisational performance, yet organisations investing in individual wellness programmes continue to report burnout, disengagement and absenteeism. This conceptual paper, based on a selective narrative review, asks whether well-being can be sustained through isolated programmes or requires a shift in organisational culture. It argues that leadership behaviour, psychological safety, communication, autonomy and work design shape well-being more than discrete programmes do. The paper proposes a four-level framework linking individual wellness, interpersonal relationships, leadership practices and organisational systems, with five testable propositions, and recommends evaluating outcomes such as psychological safety, engagement and retention rather than participation. It concludes that lasting well-being must be embedded in policies, management practice and leadership behaviour, so that organisations move from providing wellness to enabling people to thrive.

This is an accepted article with a DOI pre-assigned that is not yet published.Middle school educators face a daunting instructional paradox: navigating the rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) while working under broad, compliance-driven district policies that overlook the distinct developmental realities of early adolescence. Early adolescents are undergoing rapid neurological growth and identity construction, meaning that a purely restrictive approach to AI misses a vital opportunity to foster critical thinking and self-regulation. To bridge the gap between high-level policy and daily classroom reality, this practitioner perspective introduces the ETHOS framework, which guides AI evaluation through five tenets: Ethical, Transparent, Human-centered, Opportunity-focused, and Safe. This playbook details how our district operationalized ETHOS into an actionable framework that shifts school cultures away from a compliance scanner and toward a developmental lens. We outline a professional development sequence that uses thinking routines, ambiguous case studies, and disciplinary breakouts to build educator capacity. Crucially, we unpack the practical distinction between AI-enhanced and AI-dependent learning, demonstrating how structured AI scaffolding preserves “productive struggle” and honors the whole child. Finally, we share honest implementation friction points and discuss how the framework remains adaptable for resource-constrained schools seeking digital equity. Ultimately, this perspective provides a ground-level roadmap for school leaders to move from abstract technology policy to responsive classroom praxis.

On November 16, 2026, Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), working with Mandiant, published findings that mark an important development in the operational use of artificial intelligence in cyber operations. https://x.com/i/status/2123457542345179163 GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent framework calledexploit_agent. The framework integrated multiple frontier and locally hosted largelanguage models and was configured to continuously analyse software patches, identify potential vulnerabilities, draft exploits and execute them automatically, without human intervention at those stages. This finding moves the discussion of agentic artificial intelligence beyond theoreticalconcerns. The central issue is no longer simply whether AI can generate sophisticated code or assist ahuman attacker. It is whether an AI agent can autonomously transform an objective into asequence of consequential operations, interact with external systems, evaluate executionresults and continue acting at machine speed. This paper examines that development and proposes a different architectural approach:ST-T1024 Agentic Architecture, documented through A1–A16. Its fundamental principle is that an agent may exercise autonomy within a human-definedoperational perimeter, without acquiring authority to redefine that perimeter. The human defines the knowledge library, permissible goals, actions, permissions, execution constraints and verification requirements. The agent operates within those specifications. The proposition is not that autonomous execution must be eliminated. It is that autonomous execution must be separated from autonomous authority. THE AGENT MAY EXECUTE. IT MUST NOT BECOME THE AUTHOR OF ITS OWNAUTHORITY.

documents.abstract: The European Union published the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) in a strategic effort to align the development and application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the common market. This act, one of the first laws of its kind, strengthened the development of trustworthy and human-centered AI through new regulations, prescribing requirements that providers of AI systems must conform to. The Act prescribes model-level technical requirements for high-risk AI systems, such as in terms of accuracy, robustness and fairness, which are to be addressed and reported in the form of conformity assessments. We identify, however, a significant gap between the high-level legal descriptions provided in the law and the low-level requirements needed for the implementation of automated assessment tools for algorithmic auditing. This gap is a major obstacle in the operationalization of AI Act compliance. The difficulties are aggravated due the lack of harmonized AI standards and the existing heterogeneity of AI models, datasets, and tasks. To address this gap, we present an open-source proof-of-concept assessment tool to operationalize the technical requirements of the AI Act according to the current regulatory landscape. With this tool, we demonstrate a bottom-up interpretation of the technical requirements of the AI Act for an automated evaluation of accuracy, robustness, and fairness. We apply our work to two neural network-based healthcare applications and discuss the requirements for further integration to initial conformity assessment and to extended application to post-market monitoring and other algorithmic auditing frameworks. With further work, the base structure presented here can be applied for integration beyond healthcare to other AI high-risk application domains.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Continuous assessment of human trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally a latent-state identification problem: trust cannot be observed directly, while its behavioral manifestations are noisy, multimodal, and often shared with other internal states such as cognitive load, uncertainty, and attention. This work introduces trustiness as an operational latent variable for characterizing the time-varying trust-related state of a user interacting with an AI system. Rather than treating behavioral measurements as direct proxies for trust, we formulate their relationship with trustiness within a multimodal state-space framework that explicitly separates latent trust, cognitive load, contextual factors, and noisy observations. Candidate gaze, head-motion, and interaction-derived features are characterized through marginal, conditional, and incremental mutual information to determine which observables retain trust-related information after accounting for confounding and multimodal redundancy. The resulting informative observation set is integrated into a recursive latent-state estimator, instantiated through an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for continuous inference. In a controlled study with 60 participants, gaze entropy, revisit behavior, verification actions, response latency, and inspection time provided the strongest independent trust-related evidence, while conditioning on cognitive load substantially reduced several otherwise apparent associations. The selected multimodal model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.112, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.149, and a Pearson correlation of 0.79 with self-reported trust across all 60 participants, evaluated on post-calibration interactions after participant-specific Trustiness Calibration Experiment (TCE) calibration. Participants were held out from population-level feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Calibration was conclusive for 57 of 60 participants, for whom the corresponding MAE was 0.108, RMSE was 0.143, and Pearson correlation was 0.81. Joint modeling of trustiness and cognitive load reduced MAE by 18.2% relative to a trustiness-only model in the conclusive-calibration evaluation, while conditional feature selection improved generalization compared with the complete unfiltered observation set. Temporal experiments further showed coherent degradation and recovery of the inferred latent state following controlled changes in AI reliability. These results indicate that continuous trust assessment is better formulated as the identification of a partially observable latent state from confounded multimodal evidence than as direct prediction from behavioral proxies, providing a mathematical framework for multimodal trust estimation in human–AI interaction.

Ergonomic risk management in electronics manufacturing still relies largely on manual, periodic inspections that offer little continuous visibility of operators' postural exposure. This case study reports the design, implementation and pilot-line validation of a Web-based ergonomic monitoring platform at an electronics manufacturing plant in Manaus, Brazil, developed over a seven-month applied research and development cycle (January–July 2026) by a technology institute in partnership with the manufacturer. The platform detects operators in industrial camera streams with a YOLOv8l detector, extracts body and hand landmarks with MediaPipe Pose and Hand Landmarker, computes joint angles, classifies each monitored joint into safe, light, moderate or high-risk angle bands with ordinal scores, and raises an alert only when a high-risk angle persists beyond a configurable holding time. Angle bands and persistence rules were defined with an NR-17-oriented ergonomics consultancy and are editable through the interface. Events flow through a containerised micro-service pipeline (RTSP ingestion, RabbitMQ messaging, REST API, SQL Server) to a Web interface with real-time monitoring, dashboards, PDF reports and a 3-D skeleton view. On a 500-frame sample from the surface-mount technology line, compared with human inspection, operator detection achieved 94.5% precision, 98.2% recall and a 96.3% F1-score; the reported hit rate on critical joints was 91.8% and the continuous hand-tracking rate 89.4%. Between 22 May and 5 August 2026 the platform recorded 409,527 alert events, with a mean uninterrupted tracking persistence of 72.0 s at 15 frames per second and a mean joint angle of 129.14° for high-risk events. Under approximately 250 concurrent requests the pipeline sustained 1.64 frames per second with about 650 ms end-to-end latency and no critical failures during a 152 s stress run, and the system passed formal acceptance testing with zero open issues (self-assessed Technology Readiness Level 6). The case shows that pose-based joint-angle alerting can be integrated into a live industrial IT environment, but also that the evidence produced does not yet establish ergonomic validity: no comparison with RULA/OWAS expert scoring, no joint-angle error against a reference measurement and no health-outcome data were obtained. These gaps define the agenda for moving from prototype to deployment.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Generative AI changes a basic condition of interactive surfaces and spaces (ISS): visitor-facing content can be produced during interaction rather than fully authored before it. We report a longitudinal qualitative study with 23 Chinese science museum practitioners, interviewed annually from 2023 to 2026 (retention 23 to 19) and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants’ accounts moved from anticipated epistemic and operational risks, through backstage experimentation and visitor-facing trials, toward situated governance and renewed questions about the purpose of museum interaction. Following these changes over time shows how generative AI reconfigured the design problems of museum ISS: generated content appeared under institutional authority; inference delay became publicly and bodily experienced; concurrent touch, gesture, and speech created ambiguous multi-user intent; and post-generation editing could leave curators selecting within an AI-defined possibility space. We conceptualize the resulting shift as a movement from prefabricated display to situated generation and formulate four design propositions concerning provenance at the point of display, spatially appropriate fallback, multi-intent negotiation, and curatorial control before generation. These propositions are grounded in practitioner accounts rather than evaluations of implemented solutions.

documents.abstract: Digital transformation is increasingly experienced not as a bounded program of organizational change but as a condition of recurrent and overlapping adaptation. Research has clarified many technological, strategic, and employee-level consequences of this shift, yet it has paid less attention to a leadership-specific problem: the possibility that leaders can continue to look effective while progressively losing the cognitive, emotional, temporal, and recovery resources required to remain effective. This conceptual paper develops a leadership-specific process theory of quiet cracking under continuous digital transformation. Rather than claiming a wholly new strain construct, the paper refines the emerging quiet-cracking literature by specifying a distinctive leadership configuration in which preserved short-term role enactment coexists with hidden resource erosion. Conservation of Resources theory provides the primary explanatory engine, while role theory, Job Demands-Resources theory, compensatory-control theory, emotional-labor research, recovery theory, and Restricted Employee Sustainability Theory are integrated to explain the process. The model proposes that continuous digital transformation intensity generates experienced transformation load; that resource loss and institutionalized recovery deficits translate this load into leadership quiet cracking; and that the dual position of leaders as change recipients and change agents, together with change-champion emotional labor, accelerates depletion. Compensatory effort can preserve visible performance and create a detection lag between internal deterioration and external failure. Adaptive leadership resilience and recovery-supportive organizational resources can slow this trajectory, but persistent overload can produce a resilience-masking loop in which resilient performance delays corrective action until buffering capacity saturates. The paper contributes a temporal and role-specific explanation of hidden leader deterioration and positions human sustainability as a boundary condition of digital agility.
